questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Describe the evolutionary changes undergone by the septal neck, siphuncle and suture lines of cephalopods.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Cephalopods** (class Cephalopoda, phylum Mollusca) have a chambered, usually coiled shell, divided into chambers by partitions called **septa**. The animal lives in the last (living) chamber and the earlier chambers are filled with gas, giving buoyancy. A thin tube, the **siphuncle**, runs through all the chambers; where it passes through a septum the septum is drawn out into a tube, the **septal neck**; and the line where a septum meets the inner wall of the shell is the **suture line**. These three features changed during the evolution of the group, from the **Cambrian-Ordovician nautiloids** to the **Devonian-Cretaceous ammonoids**, and they are used to identify and date the fossils.

**1. Evolution of the septal neck.**

- In the **earliest nautiloids** (Late Cambrian) the septal necks were **short and curved**, and the siphuncle tube was made of such short, curved collars.
- In many **Ordovician and Silurian straight-shelled nautiloids** (the orthocones) the necks became **long and straight (tubular)**, directed backward, so that the siphuncle was a more or less continuous, strong tube.
- In **later nautiloids** and in the living *Nautilus* the septal necks are **short and recurved (directed backward)**.
- In the **ammonoids** (goniatites, ceratites and ammonites) the septal necks are **short collars**, and their orientation differs in the various groups.
- The general trend is therefore that the **length and shape of the neck changed with the group**, from curved and short, through long and straight in many early orthocones, to short in the later nautiloids and ammonoids, with a change in the strength and the function of the siphuncle.

**2. Evolution of the siphuncle.**

- In the **early nautiloids** the siphuncle was **central or nearly central**, and often **wide**, and some large forms (e.g. *Endoceras*, Ordovician) had a very large siphuncle that was **partly filled with calcareous deposits** (endosiphuncular deposits) that served as ballast to keep the shell horizontal.
- In later nautiloids the siphuncle became **narrower**, and in many (*Orthoceras*, *Nautilus*) it stayed **narrow and central** (or sub-central).
- In the **ammonoids** the siphuncle became **small, narrow and marginal**, usually at the **outer (ventral) edge** of the shell and **lying next to the outer wall of the whorls**. This shift from a central to a ventral and marginal position is one of the important differences between the nautiloids and the ammonoids.

**3. Evolution of the suture lines.** The suture line becomes **more complex with time** (probably increasing the strength of the shell against the water pressure and the area of attachment of the septa).

| Group (and age) | Suture line |
|---|---|
| **Nautiloids** (Ordovician to Recent) | **Simple**: straight or gently curved, with very slight undulations (a few shallow lobes and saddles) |
| **Goniatites** (Devonian to Permian) | **Zigzag**: a **simple pattern of a few undivided lobes** (pointing backward, towards the apex) and **undivided, rounded saddles** (pointing forward, towards the aperture) |
| **Ceratites** (Triassic) | **Ceratitic**: the **lobes are finely subdivided (serrated)** while the **saddles remain smooth and rounded** |
| **Ammonites** (Jurassic and Cretaceous) | **Ammonitic**: **both lobes and saddles are finely subdivided (frilled)** to give an extremely complex pattern |

(A few late Cretaceous ammonites show a simplified, ceratite-like suture again, so the trend is general, not universal.)

**Summary.** The evolution of the cephalopods shows: the **septal neck** changing from short and curved, through long and straight in many early orthocones, to short collars in the later forms; the **siphuncle** passing from wide and central to narrow and marginal; and the **suture line** progressing from simple (nautiloid) to zigzag (goniatite), to partly (ceratite) and finally fully (ammonite) subdivided. These features make the ammonites useful as **zone fossils** in the Mesozoic.

**Sketches to draw:** a longitudinal section of a nautiloid shell showing the chambers, septa, siphuncle and septal necks, and the four suture patterns (nautiloid, goniatite, ceratite and ammonite) side by side, with lobes and saddles labelled.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Distinguish between the following terms as used in stratigraphy.

(i) Diachronous and marker beds;

(ii) Diastem and disconformity.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Diachronous and marker beds.**

| | **Diachronous bed (unit)** | **Marker bed** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | A rock unit (usually a lithological unit such as a sandstone) whose **age varies from place to place**: its boundaries **cut across time planes (they are not isochronous)**. | A **thin, distinctive and widespread bed** that can be recognised easily over a wide area and that is **deposited quickly, practically at one time (isochronous)**. |
| **Cause** | It is formed by a **moving environment**, for example a **transgressing sea**: a beach sand is deposited in the sea progressively farther inland, so that it is **older where the sea first reached and younger where it reached later**. | It is formed by an **event** that has a wide effect and a geologically **instantaneous deposit**: a volcanic ash fall (tuff, bentonite), a widespread turbidite, a thin coal or limestone, or a bed rich in a particular fossil or mineral. |
| **Use** | **Cannot be used for time correlation**; correlation by lithology alone is misleading. | **A very good tool for correlation**: it provides a **time line** between sections. |

**(ii) Diastem and disconformity.** Both are breaks in sedimentation in beds that are **parallel**, but they differ in the length of the gap and in what is seen.

| | **Diastem** | **Disconformity** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | A **very short interruption** in sedimentation (from a few hours to some thousands of years) within a continuous succession; a **minor break** that is part of normal deposition. | An **unconformity between parallel beds**, in which a **significant time interval** is not represented by rock because of **non-deposition or erosion**. |
| **Erosion** | **None or very slight**. | **Clear erosion surface**, uneven, with channels or small relief, and often a basal conglomerate, a soil or weathered layer (palaeosol). |
| **Time gap** | Negligible (often cannot be detected from fossils). | **Large** (can be shown by the **absence of fossil zones**, or a change in the fossils across the surface). |
| **Evidence** | A thin parting, a ripple-marked or mud-cracked surface, a burrowed surface or a thin hardground. | A **missing fossil zone**, an irregular surface, weathered material and a **change in the fossils**. |
| **Significance** | Not a true unconformity; it marks only a small pause. | A **true unconformity**, which divides a succession into two units and records uplift or a fall in sea level. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Explain the various ways by which man can reduce the effects of earthquakes.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Earthquakes cannot be prevented, but **people can reduce the loss of life and damage** by the following measures.

1. **Earthquake-resistant design and construction.** Buildings can be made **low, light, symmetrical and flexible**, with reinforced concrete and steel frames, cross-bracing and deep strong foundations, **base isolators** and flexible joints, and **strict building codes** enforced. Old buildings, bridges and dams can be **retrofitted**.
2. **Land-use planning and hazard mapping.** Build **away from active faults, steep unstable slopes and soft, water-logged ground** that is liable to **liquefaction** and amplifies the shaking, and **build on solid bedrock**; map the hazard zones (seismic zoning), and keep open space and key services (hospitals, schools) in safe places.
3. **Monitoring, forecasting and early warning.** Networks of **seismographs**, **tiltmeters**, **GPS** and the study of **past earthquakes** to find where and how often they occur, to give **early-warning systems** that alert people seconds before the strong waves arrive, and to shut off gas, trains and lifts automatically.
4. **Preparedness and education.** **Public education and earthquake drills** (drop, cover and hold), emergency plans, stocks of food, water and first-aid, trained **rescue teams**, and a place to assemble.
5. **Reducing secondary hazards.** **Automatic gas and electrical cut-offs** and firebreaks to limit **fires**; **flood and tsunami defences** and warning systems on coasts; **slope stabilisation** against landslides.
6. **Insurance and rapid relief**, which spread the financial loss and speed up recovery.
